2. The appellant who held the post of Professor of Medicine and Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research was served with a notice issued on June 5, 1980 by Prof. M.A. Haleem, Additional Secretary-in-charge, Ministry of Health and Population Control retiring him from service with immediate effect. The notice was served in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 (Act No XII of 1974). No reason excepting the statement that the applicant completed 25 years of service appeared in the notice. In his petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the appellant prayed for declaring this notice illegal and having been made without lawful authority and also for cancelling, withdrawing and/or rescinding it. Subsequent to the issuance of the Rule the appellant amended the Writ Petition by adding the prayer for giving direction to reinstate him in the posts held by him in the Institute. 

 6. Some facts which appear in the petition may seem to be relevant for deciding the legality or otherwise of the impugned notification. The appellant completed 25 years of service on 10.4.1977. Due to scarcity of doctors restriction has been imposed on government doctors in seeking employment outside the country. For the same reason as many as 34 doctors who have completed 25 years of service have not been retired. To show the malice in law it was stated that many of these doctors were senior to the appellant in service. Further, there had been no allegations against him for inefficiency, negligence or misconduct. No reason, valid or otherwise, appears from the impugned notification for his premature retirement. The appellant completed 25 years of service more than a year before the order impugned in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 was passed. It was, therefore, claimed that the impugned notification issued on June 5, 1980 was issued for achieving collateral purposes and the order contained therein amounted to compulsory retirement. 

 In his affidavit-in-reply the appellant stated that Professor Muniruzzaman who had been put in current charge of the Office of the Director of the Institute was senior to him. 

 21. It was submitted that from the facts and circumstances stated above it would appear that the Government had no valid reason to retire the appellant from service. It was further submitted that after the judgment in the previous Writ Petition the Government should not have adversely affected the appellant's position, by issuing the notification retiring him from service altogether. The impugned notification appears to have been issued in order to circumvent that judgment. It is, therefore, mala fide as having been issued for achieving some collateral purposes. Before proceeding further I consider it necessary to refer to the provisions of both the Constitution and a few enactments including rules made thereunder, whose effect on the validity or otherwise of the impugned order has to be determined by us. 

 (b) "nationalized enterprise" includes any commercial or industrial enterprise bank, firm, tea estate or any other enterprise owned by or vested in the Government or any corporation or local authority. 

 (iv) is a contingent or work-charged employee or a worker as defined in the State-owned Manufacturing Industries Workers(Terms and Conditions of Service Ordinance, 1973 (XXIII of 1973).

 28. In support of his contention that section 9(2) of the Act is ex facie discriminatory, the learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that nowhere in the Act any principle or guideline has been laid down to regulate the exercise of power by the Government to, retire a government servant who completed 25 years of service. He took us through the preamble of the Act and provisions of sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10 of the Act. Provisions of none of these sections give any indication whatsoever as to how the government would make selection, from among the government servants who have completed 25 years, a particular government servant for retirement before he has attained the age of superannuation namely, 57 years. There should be some criteria or yardstick in the Act itself which has conferred such discretion. Such criteria or yardstick may not have been necessary if there was no question of selection of some from the many involved in the group, from which the selection has to be made. Section 9(2) clearly indicates that there is a need for classification whenever the power conferred on the Government has to be exercised in relation to a group of officers similarly situated. The learned Counsel mentioned that instead of providing any principle or guideline either in the Act or the rule the legislature has left scope for the Government to make such selection arbitrarily. As a result, not only in the impugned notification but also in the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondents no reason has been given as to why the appellant had been selected for premature retirement out of so many doctors answering the description mentioned in section 9(2) of the Act, It seems that for this reason the respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition stated that the appellant was retired from service in accordance with law. No other fact has been disclosed in the affidavit-in-opposition indicating the ground for which the appellant had been retired He further mentioned that there is no co-relation between sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of the Act Sub-section (1) gives an opportunity to Government servants to go out of government employment voluntarily, seeking an order of retirement from the Government for enabling him to do so. The exercise of such option by a government servant does not involve any other government servant in the process. So far the Government has been given the power to retire, a government servant who has completed 25 years of service, its exercise may or invariably does involve a number of government servants similarly situated. For example, in the present case, a large group of doctors who attained 25 years of service out of which only the appellant and three others were selected by the Government for early retirement were involved. 

 29. In support of the principal ground urged which relates to the invalidity of section 9(2) of the Act as being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, the learned counsel for the appellant relied on a number of decisions. To begin with reference was made to the case of Ram Krishna Dalmia vs. Justice Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 538, which considered the validity of the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 and the notification issued under section 3 of the Act by the Central Government. Mr. Ahmed drew our attention to the following passage quoted from another judgment of the Indian Supreme Court, namely Budhan vs. State of Bihar, AIR 195 SC 191: 

 32. Next, the learned Counsel for the appellant referred to the case of Waris Meah vs. The State, (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 117—PLD 1957 SC 157, which held certain provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (VII of 1947) violative of the equality clauses of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1956 as being discriminatory. The impugned provisions gave power to the Government or the State Bank to determine whether a person offending any provisions of the Act was to be tried under the ordinary law or by an Adjudication Officer or by a Tribunal. Munir C.J. who delivered the judgment of the Court observed that: 

 The Act confers discretion of a very wide character upon stated authorities, to act in relation to subjects falling within the same class in three different modes varying greatly in severity. By furnishing no guidance whatsoever in regard to the exercise of this discretion the Act, on the one hand, leaves the subject, falling within its provisions, at the mercy of the arbitrary will of such authority, and, on the other, prevents him from invoking his fundamental right to equality of treatment under the Constitution. 

 33. In distinguishing the decision pronounced by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Jibendra Kishore Achhara Chowdhury vs. The Province of East Pakistan. (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 21= PLD 1957 SC 9, Munir, C.J. observed that no analogy could be drawn between the impugned provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act and the provisions of the E. Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, whose constitutionality was challenged in the aforesaid case. The provisions of this Act which were impugned were held to be not unconstitutional as they had intended to eliminate all rent-receiving interests and to create a uniform class of tenants under the Government and that section 3 of the Act gave the power or discretion to acquire simultaneously or from time to time, the interests which were to be terminated. In rejecting the contentions that the Act in question Jibendra Kishor Achharya Chowdhury's case was on the face of it discriminatory, the Supreme Court held that: 

 "Three tribunals with different powers and procedures have been set up. The Act creating them contains no indication as to which class or classes of cases are to go before a Court and which before the Tribunal and the Adjudication Officer and it does not impose upon the Central Government, the obligation or expressly confer on it the power, of making rules with a view to classifying the cases to be tried by each of these tribunals. Nor does it define the principle or policy on which such classification may be made by the Central Government or the State Bank." 

 35. Mr. K.A, Bakr, the learned Attorney General, drew our attention to the passage which I quoted above from Jibendra Kishore's case and asserted that it gave authority for his submission that since the impugned Public Servants (Retirement) Act empowered the Government to  retire any Government servant who had completed 25 years of service, the Act could not be said to be discriminatory on the face of it, The learned Attorney-General however, could not show us how or on what principle a government servant, out of a group of so many other government servants similarly placed like him, can be elected by the Government for retirement under section 9(2) without any discrimination. In Jibendra Kishore's case the acquisition of the interests of rent-receivers was not "piece—meal but wholesale" as was pointed out by the learned Chief Justice No selection was involved. The interests of all rent-receivers throughout the province were to be acquired at one and the same time. 

 36. Even if there are discriminatory provisions in taxing statute, they will not be immune from attack on the ground of their infringement of the equality clauses in the Constitution, In support, the learned Counsel for the appellant relied on the cases of Kuntrathat Thathunni Moopil Nair Vs. State of Kerala and others, AlR 1961 SC 552, wherein it was observed that "though the Courts are not concerned with the policy underlying a taxing statute or whether a particular tax could not even be imposed in a different way or in a way the Court might think more just and equitable," it would strike down such law if it is discriminatory in its effect. In holding that the impugned provisions of the Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act, 1955 which subjected the same class of property similarly situated to an incident of taxation which resulted in in-equality, the Court observed as follows: 

 38. While referring to the reliance of the learned Judges of the High Court Division on the observations made in the case of Matajoy Dobey vs. H.C. Share, AIR 1956 (SC) 44 at p. 48 that "a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power and that abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion is vested in Government and not in a minor official", the learned Counsel submitted that the action taken against the appellant was obviously discriminatory, no reason has been offered and no fact has been stated by the Government from which the basis of the action could be discerned. The learned Counsel cited the case of Padfield vs. Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, ALL. E.R. 1968 694, in which the House of Lords had the occasion to consider the limits of the exercise of the discretionary statutory powers by a Minister and the extent of the judicial control over such exercise. 

 40. The learned Counsel referred to a few observations of the noble law Lords which, I think, are relevant to the points raised before us for our decision. One of them shows whether a Minister who is not required by law to state reasons for his decision can avoid to do so where public interest demands that he should give such reasons for the protection of persons "treated contrary to the public interest." As Lord Hodson observed: 

 44. Of the cases relied on by the learned Judges of the High Court Division first comes the case of Shyamlal vs. State of Uttar Prodesh, AIR 1954 SC 369, wherein challenge was made by the appellant against his compulsory retirement on completion of 25 years of service. Here, no ground was taken on infringement of Articles 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution which contained the equality provisions. The service rules provided that a public servant can (on completion of 25 years of service only) be compulsorily, retired in the public interest and without assigning any reason. The background against which the appellant was compulsorily retired showed that there were allegations against him and out of several charges brought against him five were established in an informal inquiry which was held after giving him the opportunity to show cause. It was held that the order of compulsory retirement was not equivalent to removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution Reasons for the decision appear in the following observations: 

 45. In the State of Bombay vs. Saubhagachand M Doshi, AIR 1957 SC 892, the Government was empowered under Service Rules to retire any Government servant on completion of 25 years of service or 50 years of age without giving any reason. The right to compulsorily retire was, however, not to be exercised except when it is in the public interest necessary to dispense with the further services of a government servant such as on account of inefficiency or dishonesty. In cases in which it was seen that the efficiency of the government servant had suffered and it was not desirable to make formal charges against him on such ground and cases were also there where corruption was being indulged in by a government servant but no specific charges were likely to be proved against him. The power of compulsory retirement could be used. No ground was urged on the violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The order of compulsory retirement was not viewed as removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Indian Constitution. 

 46. In Shiva Charana vs. State of Mysore. AIR 1965 SC 280, Government was empowered under rule 285 of the Mysore Civil Service Rules to retire compulsorily a government servant in public interest after he completed 25 years of service or attained 50 years of age, though the age of normal superannuation was fixed at 55 years. This power could be exercised if retirement was considered necessary in the public interest, provided also notice was given to the government servant concerned at least 3 months before he was required to retire. Notice, in fact, was issued to the appellant. It was held that the compulsory retirement was not removal under Article 311 and the Service Rules empowering the government to compulsorily retire a government servant did not contravene the equality provisions of the Indian Constitution. 

 47. In Tara Singh vs. the State of Rajas than, AIR 1975 SC 1487, the appellant was retired on completion of 25 years of qualifying service and notice requiring the appellant to retire with effect from the date of the expiry of 3 months from the date of the notice was served upon the appellant. In the notice mention was made that the Government was satisfied that it is in the public interest to dispense with further service of the appellant. It was contended that there was violation of Article 14 because there was no guidance as to who would be selected or on what basis the selection would be made for compulsory retirement Though rule 244(2) of the Service Rules did not specifically mention that an order was to be passed in the public interest. Notes appended to the Rules gave indication as to how the order of compulsory retirement was to be exercised. 

 "It is not usual in measures of this nature to find a carte blanche given to executive authority. In the case-law cited before us, almost all the systems codifying the rights and obligations between the State and its servants invariably contain the controlling consideration that the power to retire a Government servant prematurely must be exercised only in the public interest or on account of inefficiency or dishonesty or some similar consideration. It is difficult to appreciate why such a factor of control was not included in the constitution of the impugned provision when it was framed." 

 53. As to the contention regarding the nature of and the reason behind the impugned order, Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, emphatically asserted that though personal malafide was urged in the previous Petition, namely, Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979, which the learned Judges of the High Court Division rejected, the appellant did not consider it necessary to urge personal malafide in the present case because here malice in law had been fully established. Excepting claiming the power to make an order of compulsory retirement under section 9(2) of the Act, no other fact had been stated by the Government by way of justifying the impugned action, nor had the facts stated by the appellant been controverted by or on behalf of the Government. The Government chose to remain silent as to what was claimed to be the real reason for making the impugned order of retirement. It was stated to be to circumvent the judgment of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 which had declared the notification of November 22, 1978 purporting to relieve the appellant of the duties and designation of Professor of Medicine as having been made without any lawful authority. 

 63. The first of two cases cited by him. Roshan Lal vs. Union of India, AIR 1967 SC 1889 refer to the nature of legal relationship between the government and civil servants. In describing what is the relationship, Ramaswari, J. stated as follows: 

 64. The next case referred to by Mr. Ahmed is Dinesh Chandra Sangma Vs. State of Assam, AIR 1978 SC 17, Goswami, J. observed as follows ; 

 "Therefore, it seems to me that reference to Article 5 of the Constitution is not really relevant in the present case. It cannot be said that by leaving discretion to the Shipping Authority, he is given the position of being a law unto himself in the sense that he can decide for himself in what conditions he will grant a permit or, as the case may be, refuse a permit. There is no question of legislation at all since each case has to be considered ad-hoc in relation to the circumstances existing when it arises in the light of the requirements of the State, and in compliance with the policy laid down. That degree of description is vested in the executive inherently as a necessary condition of its existence. 

 74. After having considered the arguments of the learned Counsel and the cases cited by him in support of his contentions that section 9(2) violated Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, I am of the view that since neither the impugned provisions of the Act nor the rules containing them provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a government servant from amongst a group of government servants similarly situated and holding similar jobs, there invariably exists the scope for arbitrary exercise of such discretion. It was not the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the government cannot have or claim the power to retire a government servant after the completion of 25 years of service, though the age of superannuation has been fixed at 57, but what is of importance and consequence to the government servant concerned who is proposed to be retired on completion of 25 years of service is that the discretion of the relevant authority must be seen to have been exercised on some such principles as are discernible in Fundamental Rule 56, Notes 2, East Bengal Service Rule and Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973. Where such basis has been provided by the enunciation of such principles, whether, under the Act or Rules made under an Act or even in the note to such Rules regarding the retirement of government servants, the concerned authority before exercising its discretion, has to con-form to the principles so provided therein, Such principles may be elaborately stated, as in rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973, but even if the rules made under an Act or note appended to any rules providing retirement on the completion of 25 years merely mention that the service of such government servant who has completed 25 years is not necessary in the interest of public service or in public interest, some basis for classification or selection is discernible. Where such basis has been provided, if the government servant concerned challenges the action of government in retiring him on completion of 25 years what the Government has to do is to show that his retirement was necessary in public interest or in the interest of public service. On the other hand, the provisions of section 9(2) coupled with the omission of such basis in the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1975 leaves scope to the concerned authority to arbitrarily retire a government servant who has completed 25 years of service. Had the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Rules. 1975 provided principles as embodied in Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants ( Retirement) Rules, 1973 which were made under similar provisions of law as in section 9(2) of the Act, no challenge could perhaps have been made as to the constitutionality of the impugned provisions of this section. The existence of such principles as are found in the Rules of 1973 would have provided a complete answer to any such challenge to their constitutionality, in spite of the expression "without assigning any reason" used in section 9(2) of the Act. In such a case the authority concerned would have remained free, so as not to disclose any reason in the retirement order, but if its action in retiring a government servant was challenged as arbitrary as has been done by the appellant in the present case, the authority could have disclosed before the Court the basis of its action, 

 For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed, the order of the High Court Division is set aside and the impugned order is declared to have been made without lawful authority. There will be no order as to costs. 

 80. Appellant's case in short is that after obtaining M.B. degree from the Calcutta. University he joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon on April 10, 1952. While in service, the appellant obtained T.O.D. degree from the University of Wales and M.R.C.P. degree from Edinburg and by successive promotions he became the Professor of Medicine in 1962. On the recommendation of the Public Service Commission he was confirmed as Professor of Medicine on May 10, 1963 with effect from April 24, 1963. The appellant stated that in recognition of his academic excellence and scientific contributions in medicine he was awarded F.R.C.P London under a special clause, as he was not an M.R. C.P. of London by examination. While the appellant was serving as Professor of Medicine in the Chittagong Medical College he was appointed to act as the Joint Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. Later on the Government by the Notification dated March 31, 1967 appointed him to act as Professor of Medicine of the said Institute in addition to his duties as Joint Director. In March, 1968 Sir James Cameron, who was the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research since establishment of the Institution in 1965, left for the U.K. and appellant was put in charge of the office of the Director and Professor of Medicine by the Notification dated January 5, 1972; and by the Notification dated November 24, 1972 the appellant was appointed as the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research with effect from January 9, 1971. Appellant's further case is that due, to his meritorious service, the Government granted him the ad-hoc rank and status of Joint Secretary in 1974; and in 1975 he was given the ad-hoc rank and status of Additional Secretary During the period of 1974-75 he was the Personal Physician of the then President of Bangladesh. The appellant stated that he completed 25 years of service on April 10, 1977 By Notification No. Per 1/1M-35/78/951 dated November 22, 1978 he was relieved of his duties and designation of Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. Legality of the Notification was challenged by filing a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court Division by its judgment dated December 6, 1979 declared the Notification dated Nov. 22, 1978 to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. In view of the said declaration the appellant was restored to the position held by him, that is, Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute. Appellant's grievance is that having failed to dislodge the appellant by the Notification dated November 22, 1978 the Government issued the impugned Notification dated June 5, 1980 purporting to retire the appellant from service in exercise of the power conferred under sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974. Legality of this Notification has been challenged on the ground of the order being in contravention of the constitutional protections, and also on the ground of malafide alleging that the impugned Notification is in furtherance and fulfilment of the illegal design of not only circumventing the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 but also achieving ulterior purpose. The impugned Notification reads as under: 

 (c) indulgence by a public servant in activities prejudicial to the interest and the fundamental principles of the state; 

 85. The learned Attorney General appearing for the respondents could only rely upon the absolute authority of the President to retain a public servant in service. In other words, apart from referring to Article 134 of the Constitution containing the doctrine that a public servant holds office during the plea-sure of the President, he had no answer to the question. All the arguments of the learned Attorney-General advanced on this point practically centered on the authority of the Government provided under the impugned statute that is to say, it is an absolute rights of the government to retire any officer after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service without assigning any reason. He referred to the statement made in the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the government before the High Court Division, to the following effect: 

 "It is further stated that impugned notification was issued not with any ulterior motive or collateral or malafide purpose, but the same was issued in accordance with law." 

 86. It has already been pointed out that Act XII of 1974 provides no guideline for the discretion by the authority. The position as stated above lends full support to the arguments of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed that in the absence of any principle or guideline for the exercise of the uncontrolled and unqualified discretion under sub-section (2) of section 9, provided the scope to the authority to pick and choose and to discriminate between government servants similarly placed on completion of 25 years of service in the matter of premature retirement; and such discrimination is inherent in the Act itself. Therefore, sub-section (2) of section 9 is violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 

 87. Equality of citizens guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution: it provides that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law. The formula as stated in the Article contains the English concept of equality before the law and the American concept of equal protection of the laws. These are not independent or severable concepts in their application and will often be found to overlap each other. The principle on which the doctrine of equal protection of laws is founded is that persons in similar circumstances must be governed by the same laws. The legislative classification by itself does not offend against the principle of equal protection of the laws provided the law operates equally on all members of the said class or group. For valid legislation, classification must be reasonable for the purpose of legislation, should not be based on proper and justifiable distinction, should not be clearly arbitrary and should have all reasonable relation to the objects and to the public purpose sought to be achieved by the legislation. So, the prohibition against denial of equal protection does not preclude the legislature from confining legislation to a class or classes, prescribing different sets of rules for different classes. But the rule speaks of the conditions that classification or discrimination is not arbitrary but reasonable and rests on a real and reasonable relation to the legislation or the subject or subject thereof and that the legislation operates equally, uniformly and impartially on all persons or property within the same class. This rule has been consistently followed by the superior Courts of the sub-continent in testing validity of a statute. The Court has to see when a law is alleged to be repugnant to the rule of equality is what the object of the law is, what is the method provided therein for the achievement of that object and whether there is a reasonable relation between the method and the end intended to be achieved. " A law applying to one person or one class of persons may be constitutional if there is sufficient basis or reason for it"—Constitutional Law by Willis. 

 90. Sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 merely provides that government may at any time retire from service a public servant who has completed 25 years of service without assigning any reason. Rule, 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules 1975 is completely silent with regard to sub-section (2) of section 9. That the statute provides arbitrary, uncontrolled and unguided discretion, and the government is also fully conscious about that, is apparent from the stand taken in the affidavit-in-opposition. Paragraph 12 of the affidavit reflects the stand of the government. It has been categorically stated therein that "the impugned notification was issued in accordance with law." The statement nakedly reflects the view taken by the government in the matter of exercise of the power provided under sub-section (2) of section 9. It is obvious that the government having given the absolute discretion to retire a public servant, the action taken against the appellant should be presumed to have been taken in accordance with law. It further reflects the stand of the government that the government does not owe even a duty to explain to the Court to justify the impugned notification. 

 97. The learned Attorney-General sought to justify the action submitting that termination of service of the appellant was brought about otherwise than by way of punishment, He further submitted that since there is no stigma the action cannot be treated as a punishment. According to him, the appellant has no valid grievance to make before a Court of law, because he cannot claim the protection of Article 135 of the Constitution. In support of this contention the learned Attorney General referred to several decisions of the Indian Supreme Court laying down the principle that a government servant whose service is terminated otherwise than by way of punishment, the government servant concerned cannot claim the protection of Article 311(2) of the Constitution of India. The rule of law laid down in these decisions, in the context of the facts of these cases, does not answer the question raised in the instant case and in the background of the facts of this case. It is to be ascertained as to when an order for termination of service is inflicted by way of punishment and when it is not. It has already been stated that a government servant holding a substantive post acquires a right to hold the post until he attains the age of superannuation or is compulsorily retired, as per terms of a contract, express or implied, or a service rule. He can be removed from the post only when the post itself is abolished or he is found guilty of misconduct, negligence, inefficiency or other disqualifications in an appropriate proceeding in accordance with the service rules read with Article 135 of the Constitution. Termination of service of a government servant so appointed must be in accordance with the service rules which in its turn must be consistent with Article 135 of the Constitution. Any law or rule dealing with termination of service by retirement before the age of superannuation must be so framed as to safeguard the protections to the government servant guaranteed under the Constitution, that is, under the Fundamental Rights as well as under Article 135 of the Constitution. In support of this view reference may be made to the judgment in the case of P.L. Dhingra v. Union of India, AIR 1958 SC 36. In this case legality of the order of the General Manager of the Northern Railway reverting the petitioner from the post he was holding to his substantive post was challenged on the ground of the order being violative of Article 311(2) of the Indian Constitution. Some observations made in the judgment may be of some assistance in the present consideration of the impugned order being violative of Article 135. S.R. Das, C.J. delivering the majority judgment, observed as follows: 

 100. In this context reference may also be made to another decision of the Supreme Court of India, wherein constitutionality of the service rule providing retirement of a government servant before the age of superannuation on the completion of 25 years of service was considered. In the case of Tara Singh, etc. vs. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1975 SC 1487 legality of the orders of compulsory retirement passed against the petitioners under Rule 244(2) of the Rajasthan Service Rules was challenged on the ground of being violative of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. A.N. Ray. C.J., delivering the the judgement of the Court, noticed that although with amended service rule the expression "public interest" was omitted but the Note appended to the Rule supplied the omission. The learned Chief Justice in dismissing the petitions observed as follows: 

 106. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed referred to a list containing names of 34 doctors in the service of the Government of Bangladesh who on the relevant date when action was taken against the appellant, completed 25 years of service but no action was taken against them. Even the appellant's successor as Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research, is senior to the appellant by age and service. On this point the learned Attorney-General found it difficult to meet the argument of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed that the appellant was retired under sub-section (2) of sec. 9 of Act XII of 1974 with the ulterior object of defeating the decision given in favour of the appellant in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. All that he could submit was that along with the appellant 3 other doctors were retired. He, however, failed to point out the basis of the consideration which resulted in the retirement of the 3 doctors along with the appellant among a large number of doctors who completed 25 years of service. When the learned Attorney General was asked to point out from the affidavit-in-opposition whether any ground has been stated therein to justify the impugned action, the learned Attorney General candidly conceded that there is nothing in the affidavit-in-opposition to indicate any basis for taking the impugned action. When he was asked whether he was in a position to know the Court from the government files if there was any allegation against the appellant, the learned Attorney General frankly submitted that even government files do not indicate any allegation against the appellant. Thus the learned Attorney General simply left the Court to guess as to what could be the reason for taking the impugned action against the appellant. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed further submitted that the mala fide of government is palpable in this case. The previous notification was declared illegal on December 6, 1979, but within a short time, that is, on June 5, 1980 the impugned action was taken against the appellant, and in support of the action the Government failed to disclose any ground, even. He submitted that in this case malice has been clearly established. Malice in common acceptation means against a person, but in its legal sense it means wrongful act, done intentionally, without just cause for excuse. 

 107. Before this Court malafide in a particular person has neither been alleged nor argued. The allegations made by the appellant clearly constitute "malice in law". Malice in law means a doing of a wrongful act intentionally without just cause or excuse. The word 'intentional' refers to the doing of the act, but it does not mean that the person concerned means to be spiteful. So, to satisfy the term maliciously it is not necessary that there should have been any spite or revenge in the respondents towards the appellant. If from any indirect motive the action was taken in total disregard of the judgment in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979, the respondents must be deemed to have acted maliciously. The House of Lords in Shearer vs. Shield (1914) AC 808, while considering the question whether it was necessary for the pursuer to prove the malice in fact was in the minds of the police when they took steps which resulted in what he alleged was his false imprisonment, pointed out the distinction between "malice in fact" and "malice in law". It was in connection with an action of damages for wrongful apprehension against two Glasgow constables who had arrested the pursuer on suspicion without a warrant. Viscount Haldane, L.C. stated that question whether it was necessary for the pursuer include that malice in fact was in the minds of the police when they took steps which resulted in his false imprisonment. Viscount Haldane L.C. observed as follow: 

 "Between malice in fact and malice in law there is a broad distinction which is not peculiar to any particular system of jurisprudence. A person who inflicts an injury upon another person in contravention of the law is not allowed to say that he did so with an innocent mind; he is taken to know the law, and he must act within the law. He may, therefore, be guilty of malice in law, although so far as the state of his mind is concerned, he acts ignorantly, and, in that sense, innocently. Malice in fact is quite a different thing ; it means an actual malicious intention on the part of the person who has done the wrongful act, and it may be, in proceedings based on wrongs independent of contract, a very material ingredient in the question of whether a valid cause of action can be stated." 

 109. In view of what has been stated above I hold that sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 is ultra vires the Constitution being violative of Articles 27, 29 and 135 of the Constitution, I further hold that the impugned Notification dated June 5, 1980 issued under the said invalid provision of law causing premature retirement of the appellant from government service is illegal and void. In the result the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs,

I would add the following words: Law relating to retirement on completion of 25 years of service allowing full pensionary benefits has been in force in the sub-continent since November 15, 1919 when rule 4 of the Civil Service Rules was brought in by Resolution No. EA 1054, made by the Government of India with approval of the Secretary of State for India in Council. It reads thus: 

 This rule was in operation when the Government of India Act, 1919 came into force from December 23, 1919 and by virtue of section 96B (4) of the said Act, this rule was validated and confirmed. Consequently, article 465A of Civil Service Regulations was brought in by an amendment and since then this provision as to premature retirement has been in force although. Note (1) of this new article 465A shows that the government retains "an absolute right" to retire any officer after 25 years of service "without giving any reasons" and "no claim to special compensation" on this account would be entertained. Note (1) did not create any new right, for this right was already there. This Note came by way of a reminder that government always got this absolute right but it gave a caution that this right should not be exercised except when it is necessary in the public interest. This expression "in the public interest" has been considered to be a sufficient safeguard against arbitrary exercise of this power, when fundamental rights including "equality clauses" were guaranteed by the Constitution law relating to premature retirement came under challenge particularly in India. It was contended that Article 465A of Civil Service Regulations was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution, but this contention was althrough rejected and it was held that law relating to retirement after 25 years service with pension does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Indian Supreme Court even observed that this question is not entertainable any more. In Sivcharan vs. State of  Mysore AIR 1965 SC 280 the Indian Supreme Court held ; 

 116. (4) As, to the question whether premature retirement is violative of Article 135, excepting a passing reference, this was not pressed by the learned Counsel for the appellant. A government servant is retired with full pension after 25 years service not as a measure of punishment. It does not bear any stigma, nor any imputation is made or allegation is brought against the government servant when thus retired with pension. It cannot be ordered before completion of 25 years service which is fairly a long period for earning pension. There may be many reasons for this kind of retirement, such as loss of efficiency, bad reputation administrative exigencies or some other overriding consideration relating to policy or administration. When the public servant is being rewarded with pension, he need not be informed of the reason in the same way as he is not required to give any reason when he himself opts to retire. Government cannot retain him in service even if his service is still required in "public interest" after 25 years of service. A show cause notice for retirement will result in the starting of a departmental enquiry on specific allegation and if the allegation is proved he will be retired as a punishment, but at the same time rewarded with a pension. If the allegation is proved he will better be dismissed or removed in which case no pension will be required to be paid. In such a case the system of retirement after 25 years of service may be abolished and the age of superannuation itself, may be reduced. The Indian Supreme Court has consistently held that premature retirement is not a punishment and it does not amount to removal, in a number of cases, particularly, Shyamlal vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1954 SC 369, Shivcharan vs. State of Mysore, AIR 1965 SC 280, Bisnunarayan vs. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1965 SC 967 and Tarashing vs. State of Rajasthan AIR 1975 SC. 1487 I find no reason to take a different view in this case Section 9(2) is not violative of Article 135.
